1:
What the protest was for they answer from David's place. Calvin takes it as written to encourage the people to fight under his banner and acknowledge him entitled to their obedience: made head over God's people, and wishing to prove himself their lawful prince, David shows he had not been influenced in anything by ambition or pride, but had submitted with a quiet and humble spirit to the divine disposal. In that, he says, is a very useful lesson — to be contented with the lot God has marked out, to avoid rash undertakings, and to confine ourselves cheerfully within our own sphere instead of attempting great things. For is it not pride that leads men, at the instigation of their passions, to dare presumptuous flights and throw the world into confusion? Clarke reports two guesses at the occasion: that David wrote it to vindicate himself when Saul's courtiers accused him of affecting the crown, or that it belongs to the captivity. Keil and Delitzsch note that it designedly precedes the next psalm, having grown out of the memory of what David said when he brought home the Ark.

Spurgeon weighs what it costs to say such a thing at all. A man should be slow to make such an appeal, for the Lord is not to be trifled with, and whoever ventures on it should be sure of his case. He begins with the heart, the centre of our nature, since if pride be there it defiles everything, as mire in the spring causes mud in all the streams. It is a grand thing to know one's own heart well enough to speak before the Lord about it; and greater still if, after searching himself, a man can protest that it is not haughty — neither proud in his own opinion, contemptuous to others, nor self-righteous before the Lord; neither boastful of the past, proud of the present, nor ambitious for the future. Gill sets against that the natural state: every heart is haughty by nature, and everything in civil life makes it more so — riches and honour, birth and blood, learning, strength and beauty.

Henry finds here a piece of self-knowledge, and divides it in three. David aimed not at a high condition nor at making a figure in the world, but could have been content to spend all his days in the sheep-folds; his own brother once charged him with pride, but groundlessly. First, he had no conceited opinion of himself, humble saints being unable to think so well of themselves as others do, since the love of God reigning in the heart subdues all inordinate self-love. Second, he had neither a scornful nor an aspiring look, his eyes not lofty to envy those above or disdain those below; where there is a proud heart there is commonly a proud look, but the humble publican would not so much as lift up his eyes. Third, he did not employ himself in things above his station.

What those things were Clarke defines by the Hebrew: not merely great matters but wonderful or sublime ones, too high for him and alien from him, not belonging to a man in his situation — and he glosses the eyes to match, that he neither looked up with desire for the state of others nor down with contempt on those beneath him. Augustine hears the whole as a sacrifice offered. It is not the voice of one man singing but of the whole body of Christ, so that as it were one man speaks, and he is one who also is many; and the humility of heart professed here is itself the offering, since a troubled spirit is the sacrifice of God. If there is no sacrifice there is no Priest — but we have a High Priest in heaven who entered within the veil, and there we may offer.
2:
The word that opens the verse is elliptical, and they handle it in three ways. Ellicott calls Surely the best rendering of a phrase that literally means if not, commonly used to express strong asseveration after an oath. Gill reads it as the oath itself, or rather the imprecation — with Kimchi and Aben Ezra, if I have not so behaved, let it come to me so and so — while noting that Noldius turns it into a question, have I not composed and quieted myself? Keil and Delitzsch reject the two readings that suggest themselves first: it does not open a conditional protasis, for there is no apodosis to be found, and it does not mean but; it is asseverating, and derived from the usual formula of an oath.

Keil and Delitzsch also sort the three denials of the psalm's opening into a scheme. Pride is repudiated first as the state of the soul, then as pride of countenance and bearing, then as pride of endeavour and mode of action — for pride has its seat in the heart, finds its expression especially in the eyes, and takes great things for the sphere in which it diligently exercises itself. They are careful about the opposites: the contrary of great things is not what is little or mean but what is small, and the contrary of things too wonderful is not what is trivial but what is attainable.

The weaned child is where the writing gathers. Ellicott draws out the figure as taken from a baby's first real sorrow, when he not merely feels pain but is allowed no access to what had been his solace hitherto: he moans and frets and sobs, but at last is quieted by the love which is powerful to soothe even when it must deny — and he quotes Herbert, that if goodness lead a man not, then weariness may toss him to God's breast. On the rendering he is exact and dissatisfied: the verb translated behave means to make equal or like, so that we cannot render it I calmed and quieted my soul; but since Hebrew commonly expresses one idea by combining two verbs, I made like and I quieted my soul is an idiomatic way of saying I made as quiet as. Clarke gives the same submission a harder edge, having been under the rod of others and, when chastised, not complaining — his silence being the fullest proof that he neither murmured nor repined but received all as from the hands of a just God, foregoing many comforts he had once enjoyed without demurring. Gill takes the behaviour more outwardly, as quiet and peaceable towards all men, even his inferiors in Saul's court, giving no token of a restless or ambitious spirit. Wesley compresses the image to a line: weaned means wholly depending upon God's providence, as the poor helpless infant relies upon its mother for support.

The closing exhortation they take as the lesson drawn from the experience. Gill says that what David had done himself, and found good for him to do, he knew was good for others, and so exhorts them to hope in the Lord and wait for his salvation constantly and to the end of life — with perhaps some respect to his own friends, weary of Saul's government and impatient to see him on the throne, whom he advises to wait and take no indirect steps, but leave it with God. Clarke turns it outward to any sufferer: act all as I have done, trust in him who is the God of justice and compassion, and after you have suffered awhile he will make bare his arm and deliver you. Short as it is, he adds, this is a most instructive psalm, for he who acts as the psalmist did is never likely to come to mischief, or to do any to others.
